To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
IgG from ALS patients and anti-motoreuron IgG induce a microglial reaction targeting motoneurons in mice without initiating T cell reaction.
IgG from patients with ALS, but not disease controls, and IgG from EAGMD induce accumulation of microglia in the ventral horns of the spinal cord in mice without recruiting CD3 lymphocytes.

ALS IgG, and IgG from EAGMD guinea pigs, but not disease control IgG, induce microglia activation in the spinal cord, and that this microglial reaction is associated with the presence of IgG deposits in the spinal cord.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new mechanism of ALS pathogenesis and the possibility of a specific therapy.
the role of IgG in the pathogenesis of ALS.
a novel hypothesis that the pathogenesis of ALS may be related to a microglia reaction induced by IgG of ALS patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IgG from ALS patients can induce an inflammatory reaction in the spinal cord that targets motor neurons.
ALS IgG is not a pathogenetic factor of ALS.
the presence of IgG in the CSF is a consequence of the disease and not a cause.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ALS is an autoimmune disease targeting the ventral horn cells of the spinal cord and that the disease process is not restricted to the central nervous system.

the IgG from ALS patients and the IgG from guineapigs with EAGMD are pathogenic to the motor neurons of the spinal cord of normal mice and that the pathogenic IgG in ALS is directed against antigens of the motor neuron cytoskeleton and not against myelin antigens.
ALS IgG induces microglia reaction in the spinal cord, which may be involved in the pathogenesis of ALS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ALS IgG can induce microglial reaction in the CNS of mice without inducing T cell response.

the ALS IgG and the anti-motoneuronal IgG from guineapigs with experimental autoimmune gray-matter disease induce a microglia response targeting motor neurons without inducing a T cell response in mice, and this is consistent with a previous report showing that ALS IgG induces an immune response in mice without inducing T cell response.
IgG from ALS and from EAGMD can recruit microglial cells into the spinal cord of recipient animals, but the T cell response is not evoked in these mice.
